claims.text: The quaternary equiatomic alloy is a single-phase FCC solid solution.
Plastic deformation under uniaxial tension will be dominated by dislocation glide on {111}<110> slip systems.
Deformation twins and stacking faults will accompany dislocation glide.
Twins and stacking faults will be especially prevalent at lower temperatures or higher strain rates.
Yield strength will be governed by solid-solution strengthening arising from lattice distortion.
Dislocation forest hardening will govern yield strength.
At very high strain rates or cryogenic temperatures, yield strength may become insensitive to strain rate when deformation transitions to athermal twin nucleation.
Yield strength may become insensitive to strain rate after dislocation-density saturation when the dislocation mean free path is limited by grain boundaries.
Rapid solidification or severe plastic deformation would likely produce fine grains and a high dislocation density, whereas casting and annealing would likely produce coarse grains.
High configurational entropy causes severe lattice distortion that increases Peierls stress and promotes cross-slip or twinning.
At low temperatures, reduced thermal activation of dislocation climb and cross-slip favors twinning as a secondary strain-accommodation mechanism.
The alloy will exhibit high yield strength together with significant ductility.
Interactions between dislocations and twins will produce continuous strain hardening.
Cooling will cause a transition from slip-dominated to twinning-dominated deformation.
Yield strength will increase with decreasing temperature and increasing strain rate.
Strain-rate sensitivity will diminish at cryogenic temperatures because twinning becomes the dominant athermal mechanism.
Decomposition into BCC, HCP, or intermetallic secondary phases may shift deformation toward brittle fracture or transformation-induced plasticity.
Nanoprecipitates could significantly alter hardening behavior.
Conventional FCC alloys such as Cu and Ni, and standard stainless steels, generally have lower yield strength and less strain hardening than FCC HEAs.
Observation of dominant FCC-to-HCP transformation rather than glide or twinning would falsify the proposed deformation mechanism.
